result: Continuous multi-day wearable HRV was lower in 127 long COVID patients than 21 controls during daily activities and sleep, and stayed depressed longer after exercise at or above VT1, proposed as a PEM threshold.
reason: Same measure (lower HRV) but in long COVID with an exercise-recovery time course, so extends rather than replicates the ME/CFS finding.

result: Wearable HRV was lower in long COVID (n=127) than controls (n=21), with delayed post-exercise recovery above VT1.
reason: Finding is about orthostatic testing (OH, POTS) and MSNA; HRV is not that measure and the paper is already linked via neuro-hrv.

result: In 108 hospitalised COVID survivors at about 9 months, IVIM diffusion MRI showed lower microvascular perfusion fraction in ICU vs ward survivors (cGM p=.032, NAWM p=.008, WMH p=.014), and lower NAWM perfusion fraction with more cognitive complaints (p=.047).
reason: Measures cerebral microvascular perfusion by IVIM, not BBB leakage or serum BBB markers; ICU vs ward comparison with no healthy or ME/CFS controls, so no atlas finding fits.

result: In a sham-controlled randomised trial of 57 post-COVID POTS patients, 1 month of low-level tragus stimulation reduced the supine-to-stand HR rise and average/max HR, lowered plasma NPY, and increased HF and decreased LF and LF/HF HRV.
reason: Treatment trial domain: no atlas finding covers auricular vagus nerve stimulation in POTS or long COVID.

result: In 115 prospectively followed COVID patients (24 months), cortisol was not associated with PCC overall, though the cognitive-symptom cluster had lower cortisol.
reason: Independent cohort with no overall cortisol difference supports the finding that low cortisol has not held up; the subgroup signal mirrors Dalhuisen's inconsistent subgroups. Sampling time is not stated and n is small.

result: In 404 SARS-CoV-2-positive and 105 negative non-hospitalised youths, SARS-CoV-2 positivity was a minor risk factor for 6-month fatigue; baseline symptom severity was the main predictor and correlated with psychosocial factors (loneliness, neuroticism) rather than biomarkers.
reason: Agrees that early symptom severity predicts fatigue, but finds psychological factors relevant and biomarkers not predictive, against the finding's claim that cytokine response matters and psychological factors do not.

result: Meta-analysis: PEM prevalence in community-dwelling adults with PCC was 25% (95% CI 17-36%; 10 studies, 4,076 participants); 7 of 8 tailored-rehab studies (1,080 patients) found no exercise-related PEM, with all studies at high risk of bias.
reason: Reports PEM prevalence and rehab response in long COVID, not PEM onset, duration or recovery timing.

result: Pooled PEM prevalence in PCC was 25% (95% CI 17-36%) across 10 studies.
reason: Does not measure ME/CFS criteria incidence or long-term course after COVID; the paper is handled by the lc-pem-prevalence retarget.

result: In 526 long COVID adults at a median 36 months, 71.9% had COMPASS-31 of 20 or more, and 33% of the cohort (40.5% of those with dysautonomia) had a new POTS diagnosis; female sex and joint hypermobility raised risk.
reason: Adds long-term persistence and POTS as the commonest diagnosis in long COVID, though the burden is mainly self-reported (online survey, active stand in a subset only).

result: Joint hypermobility was associated with higher risk of autonomic dysfunction in a 526-person online long COVID cohort.
reason: A long COVID version of the hypermobility link, like Lubell 2026, but the outcome is autonomic dysfunction, likely by self-report, and the abstract gives no effect size.
